s: This document is the three-act play Dandy Dick. It centers on Augustin Jedd, Dean of St. Marvells, whose efforts to preserve dignity, fund the restoration of the Minister Spire, and control his household are undone by racing, betting, disguises, and misunderstandings. His daughters, Salome and Sheba Jedd, want to attend a masked ball with Gerald Tarver and Nugent Darbey, but their expensive dresses expose the family’s lack of ready money. The Dean has committed £1,000 to the Restoration Fund and must retrench. His widowed sister, Georgiana Tidman, formerly the racehorse owner George Tidd, arrives and proves a disruptive force, co-owning the racehorse Dandy Dick with Sir Tristram Mardon and secretly planning to bet on him. Georgiana agrees to stake Salome’s and Sheba’s money on Dandy Dick. At the Deanery, the Dean’s public offer brings seven wealthy donors to promise £1,000 each, making his own obligation urgent. When the Swan Inn burns, Dandy Dick is rescued and hidden in the Deanery stables. Georgiana persuades the reluctant Dean to bet £50 on the horse for the Restoration Fund. Edward Blore, sent to place the wager, secretly puts strychnine in Dandy Dick’s bolus in an attempt to keep him from racing, while mistakenly betting the Dean’s money on Bonny Betsy. Meanwhile, the girls return from the cancelled ball with Tarver and Darbey, who have arrived disguised as shabby Cavaliers. The confusion culminates when the Dean is arrested after being found administering medicine to Dandy Dick. At the police station, Hannah Topping recognizes him as her former master and tries to help him, but Noah Topping repeatedly mistakes events and adds charges against him. In the final return to the Deanery, the Dean is rescued and the various secrets emerge. Salome and Sheba have won fifty pounds at the races and accepted Tarver and Darbey; Georgiana has won £1,500 on the Handicap. The strychnine is traced to Blore, whose confession clears the Dean of poisoning the horse, though it reveals the Dean’s own concealed betting. Noah’s final accusation also collapses. Georgiana concludes that the Dean’s deceptions have damaged his authority, but offers help for the Spire through George Tidd. The play ends with the household accepting friendly laughter at the Dean’s folly.
