s: Dr. Jedd, also called Augustin and the Dean of St. Marvells, is a widowed father of Salome and Sheba, brother of Georgiana Tidman, and resident master of the Deanery. He is institutionally aligned with the Bishop of St. Marvells and concerned with the Minister Spire’s restoration. Though he has unpaid bills and no spare cash for his daughters’ dresses, he conditionally pledges one thousand pounds to the Restoration Fund if seven others match it. When seven wealthy donors do so, his obligation becomes pressing. Georgiana comes to live at the Deanery, embarrassing the dignified Dean through her racing language, manners, and association with Dandy Dick. He fears both her influence and the approaching races. After the Swan Inn burns, Georgiana seeks to house Dandy Dick at the Deanery; the Dean objects but cannot prevent Dandy Dick and Sir Tristram from staying. Financial pressure over the Spire leads him to let Georgiana place a fifty-pound bet on Dandy Dick through his long-serving butler, Edward Blore. Believing he is humanely treating a suffering horse’s chills, Dr. Jedd prepares and administers a veterinary bolus to Dandy Dick. It is taken as an attempt to give the horse an unfair advantage, and Blore identifies him as the supposed villain. Arrested in the Deanery stables for trespassing, handcuffed, and taken to the lock-up, he is also associated with accusations over Dandy Dick’s treatment and the Swan Inn fire. His disappearance alarms others; his family influence seems lost and his cherished dignity crushed. In the cell, Hannah recognizes and briefly frees him, but he refuses escape from conscience and concern for dignity. Noah recaptures him. Once identified as the Dean rather than an unknown intruder, he mildly accepts Noah’s error, withdraws any charge against the person found on his premises, and invites Noah and Hannah to dinner.

l: Major Tarver, Dandy Dick
s: Major Tarver is a middle-aged Army officer and gentleman in the Hussars, an invalid with an unstable liver whose excitement alternates with depression. At the Deanery, he helps arrange the evening and the girls’ costumes, plans to attend the ball as Charles the First, and loves Salome Jedd passionately. After dinner he suffers indigestion, loses the music for his intended song, and leaves when the Swan Inn fire is controlled. Later, shabby and miserable in his Cavalier costume, he carries a carriage umbrella, says the Military were summoned to St. Marvells, and begs Salome to smile on him again. Finally, weak and supported by Mr. Darbey, he claims rejection will ruin his health and is accepted by Salome.

l: Mr. Darbey, Dandy Dick
s: Mr. Darbey, Nugent Darbey, is a young, pompous Hussar lieutenant, officer, gentleman, and violin player, though also classified as a civilian in the military-civilian distinction. He loves and is attracted to Sheba Jedd. He first visits the Deanery with Gerald Tarver, helps arrange the girls’ attendance at a ball, and plans to appear as Charles the Martyr. He patronizes and quarrels with the Dean, plays violin with Sheba accompanying, resents Major Tarver’s singing, and later returns for his violin. In shabby Cavalier dress, he says the ball was cancelled and guards the ruined Swan Inn with Tarver. Finally, he brings Major Tarver to Salome and Sheba, then proposes to Sheba; after reflection, she accepts.

l: Blore, Dandy Dick
s: Blore is the venerable-looking butler and servant of Augustin, the Dean, working in the Deanery household. He is acquainted with Hannah Topping and gambles on horse races, both for himself and on commission for the kitchen. Hoping Bonny Betsy will win, he stakes his savings and then the Restoration Fund money on that horse. After taking the Dean’s fifty pounds to bet on Dandy Dick, he secretly puts strychnine in Dandy Dick’s bolus. He later visits Hannah at the police station, worried about the case’s effect on the Dean and Dandy Dick. Blore finally confesses his betting and poisoning; the Dean retains him in service in return for silence.

l: Georgiana, Dandy Dick
s: Georgiana Tidman, Mrs. Tidman, is the widowed younger sister of Augustin Jedd, the Dean, aunt of Salome and Sheba, and resident guest at the Deanery. A high-spirited but self-described feeble woman with a keen sense of right and wrong, she is devoted to horse racing, gambling on races, and her half-share in Dandy Dick. After her husband's death she continued his career as a horse-breeder and gentleman jockey under the racing name George Tidd, wearing crimson and black diamonds; she ultimately lost her horses and property. At the Deanery she arrives in masculine racing dress, declares her ownership interest in Dandy Dick, plans to bet every penny on him, and persuades others to stake money on the horse despite promising not to own one while among the Canons and Bishop. She serves tea while studying betting, rushes to save horses during the Swan Inn fire, shelters Dandy Dick in the Deanery stables, and worries over his singed tail during the storm. She presses the Dean to wager on Dandy Dick to aid the Spire, organizes food and champagne for the horse, and protects Salome and Sheba. She accompanies Sir Tristram in seeking the missing Dean, helps rally race-course associates to rescue him from the Hill, and wins fifteen hundred pounds on the Handicap. She becomes engaged to Sir Tristram and helps reveal Blore's strychnine in the bolus. At the end, she rebukes the Dean for deception and lost dignity, while offering George Tidd's thousand-pound loan for the Spire if he accepts being laughed at as a Sporting Dean.

l: the Deanery, Dandy Dick
s: The Deanery of St. Marvells is the residence of Dr. Jedd, the Dean, and home to Salome and Sheba. It includes a morning-room with a piano, stables, an old nursery available for lodging, and a kitchen, and it employs Deanery servants. It begins as the site of visits by Gerald Tarver and Nugent Darbey for ball plans and the expected arrival of Georgiana Tidman. Georgiana arrives as Augustin’s widowed sister, reunites with Augustin and Sir Tristram, and imagines remaining through the autumn meeting. The Deanery then hosts dinner and an evening gathering of tea, violin playing, and news of the Restoration Fund. After the Swan Inn fire, its stables shelter Dandy Dick, while the old nursery houses Sir Tristram. Smoking, the horse, gambling, and Georgiana’s conduct disrupt the Dean’s formerly respectable peace. Later, the household responds to an arrest and expected visit, the Dean is brought home and calls for comfort, the masked-ball attendance of his daughters is exposed, and Noah traces an unknown man there. The kitchen is offered to Noah and Hannah for lodging and dinner.

l: St. Marvells, Dandy Dick
s: St. Marvells is a locality with little serious crime, a police station, and a small class of expected offenders; it returns a Conservative. Augustin Jedd is Dean, and Noah becomes Head Constable after arriving with Hannah. On the eve of races there, Georgiana arrives at the Deanery, troubling Augustin.

l: Durnstone, Dandy Dick
s: Durnstone is a place containing the Athenaeum and the destination police station. It hosts a Fancy Dress Masked Ball, with Gerald Tarver and Nugent Darbey stationed there, and Georgiana Tidman stays at the Wheatsheaf. Later Noah plans to take a prisoner and the Dean there, where the Bench sits and the Dean’s case can be reported.

l: Durnstone Athenaeum, Dandy Dick
s: The Durnstone Athenaeum is where Salome and Sheba arrived expecting the ball, only to find a notice on the front door announcing its cancellation.

l: Fancy Dress Masked Ball at Durnstone, Dandy Dick
s: The Fancy Dress Masked Ball at Durnstone, promoted by the Officers of the Hussars, is planned for one night, with Salome and Sheba intending to attend secretly with Gerald Tarver and Nugent Darbey. Although a notice says it is cancelled after the Military are summoned to St. Marvells, it ultimately takes place; Salome and Sheba attend in French Revolution lady and flower-girl costumes.

l: St. Marvells Spring Meeting, Dandy Dick
s: The races at St. Marvells are scheduled for the following day and are a source of anxiety for Augustin because of Georgiana's racing interests. Georgiana and Sir Tristram discuss Dandy Dick's chances in connection with them. The Races are attended by Georgiana, Salome, and Sheba, with Georgiana winning fifteen hundred pounds over the Handicap and the girls winning fifty pounds. Dandy Dick wins, while Bonny Betsy loses.

l: Durnstone Handicap, Dandy Dick
s: The Durnstone Handicap is a horse race scheduled for the following day. Dandy Dick, ridden by Tom Gallawood at nine stone two, and Bonny Betsy are contenders. Georgiana believes Dandy Dick has backed himself and worries cold water may have hurt his chances, though his singed tail reduces his carried weight. Despite ten-to-one odds against Dandy Dick, he is seen as strong, while Blore favors Bonny Betsy.

l: the Restoration Fund, Dandy Dick
s: The Restoration Fund supports Minster Spire restoration. In the second act, it benefits from the Dean’s public thousand-pound offer, prompting seven wealthy donors to give matching sums; the Dean also directs a wager expected to add five hundred pounds toward the Spire.

l: the Minister Spire, Dandy Dick
s: The Minster Spire, somewhat out of repair, faces crumbling unless restoration begins immediately. The Dean, its principal creditor, offers a thousand-pound loan for preservation or repair, while Georgiana proposes using Dandy Dick’s race winnings to help fund the work.

l: the scandalous costumes, Dandy Dick
s: Dresses made in London from patterns as a French Revolution gown and flower-girl outfit arrive as cast-off clothing, cost forty pounds nineteen shillings, and are raffled for local charities.

l: the account for the fancy dresses, Dandy Dick
s: The account for the fancy dresses is a cash bill from Lewis Isaacs, Costumier to the Queen, for costumes hired for the masked ball at Durnstone. It totals forty pounds, nineteen shillings, including fifteen guineas for Salome’s gown, ten guineas for Sheba’s costume, trimmings, extras, and mislaid brown-paper patterns. Salome and Sheba owe the bill without Augustin’s knowledge and possess only fifteen shillings and threepence, so they seek Georgiana’s help to win money. The Dean, himself unable to settle his bills, later discovers the account and demands that the girls explain it; they promise to pay with their winnings.

l: retrenchment, Dandy Dick
s: is_a household policy [advocated by Dr. Jedd] Dr. Jedd says that the family's spending on clothes and other bills must be stopped and summarizes the solution as 'Retrench and Rejoice.' He hopes Georgiana Tidman will help impose the precepts of retrenchment.

l: the family finances, Dandy Dick
s: are_limited considerably under five hundred pounds [immediately commandable by Dr. Jedd] The family finances are strained by £156, 18 shillings and 3 pence in existing bills and by the costly dresses. Dr. Jedd says that he can immediately command considerably under £500, while he has pledged £1,000 to the Minister Spire restoration fund if seven other donors match it.

l: Sir Tristram, Dandy Dick
s: Sir Tristram is a bachelor, former Oxford associate and friend of Augustin Jedd, and a horseman/racing enthusiast. He stays at the Swan Inn with his horse, is a guest at the Deanery, habitually smokes a pipe, and co-owns the racehorse Dandy Dick, holding one half. Visiting Augustin, he eagerly discusses Dandy Dick's prospects in the Durnstone Handicap and learns that Georgiana, formerly George Tidd, owns the other half; they agree the horse is fit and likely to win. After Dandy Dick is rescued from the Swan Inn with a singed tail after cold water has been thrown over him, Sir Tristram and Georgiana arrange to move him to the Deanery stables. During a storm at the Deanery, Sir Tristram shares Georgiana's concern for the horse and hides with her to watch suspicious movement in the garden. He confronts Darbey and Tarver, questions Hatcham about the person who set fire to the inn, accompanies Georgiana to the police-station, dictates a description of the missing Dean, and helps plan and carry out the Dean's release and rescue. Learning that a bolus contained strychnine, he denounces the Dean. He proposes to Georgiana and is accepted. Finally, he helps show that the person secured in the stable is not the Dean and tells the Dean that there is no harm in laughter.

l: the Swan Inn, Dandy Dick
s: The Swan Inn is a place destroyed by fire. In the evening it catches fire; its horses are cleared out and Dandy Dick is rescued, with Georgiana proposing the Deanery stables. It is then reduced to guarded ruins.

l: Dandy Dick, Dandy Dick
s: Dandy Dick is a sporting racehorse owned jointly by Sir Tristram Mardon and Georgiana Tidman. Wearing black-and-white colors with a pink cap and ridden by Tom Gallawood, he is entered in the Durnstone Handicap, also called Dandy Dick’s handicap. Sir Tristram considers him fit and properly weighted, while Georgiana, confident from knowing him thoroughly, buys a half share and bets on him. After a fire at the Swan Inn, where he had been stabled, he is rescued safe but cold and with a singed, later reported lost, tail. He is sheltered in the Deanery stables, feeds steadily, and is treated cautiously for a possible chill while remaining a favored contender, ahead of Bonny Betsy according to the Dean. His prospects are endangered when Blore secretly adds strychnine to his bolus; reports then reveal that he was being nobbled and had been dosed, though the chemist’s analysis is pending. Despite these dangers, Dandy Dick runs and wins the Races in a common canter, after the Dean has instructed Blore to back him for the Restoration Fund.

l: Bonny Betsy, Dandy Dick
s: A horse handicap-race entrant loses the Races, finishing behind Dandy Dick with the policeman, after Blore plans to remove Dandy Dick but mistakenly wagers on her.

l: horse racing, Dandy Dick
s: is_a sport Horse racing has been a major part of Georgiana's past and remains an interest she cannot abandon. She says that she cannot live without horseflesh and continues to understand racing form, colors, stables, and betting despite promising Augustin that she would not own anything on four legs.

l: betting on Dandy Dick, Dandy Dick
s: is_intended_to_win the thousand-pound wager [Georgiana Tidman's stated ambition] Georgiana decides to bet every penny she has on Dandy Dick after judging that he is fit to win. She then agrees to let Salome and Sheba stake their limited money on him in hopes of covering their debt.

l: the thousand-pound wager, Dandy Dick
s: Georgiana Tidman proposes a thousand-sovereign wager tied to becoming richer by the next night and to her position in the Deanery. Alongside this, a race wager using the Dean’s fifty pounds was meant to back Dandy Dick for the Restoration Fund, but Blore placed it on Bonny Betsy.

l: Hatcham, Dandy Dick
s: Hatcham is a groom and stable man. He watches Dandy Dick overnight, carries Dandy’s dose, and reports that the villain who burned the Swan Inn was caught administering it and taken by constable to the lock-up.

l: the Military, Dandy Dick
s: is_summoned_to St. Marvells The Military were summoned to St. Marvells, preventing the ball from taking place. Darbey and Tarver say they were responding to the call of duty.

l: the dinner, Dandy Dick
s: is_a dinner [hot and served with ale] The dinner at the Deanery is called a success, although the mutton is overdone, the potatoes rattle, the custards are a first attempt, and the chimney appears to need sweeping. The guests are mostly silent, and the women jokingly describe it as a frightfully jolly dinner.

l: the fire at the Swan Inn, Dandy Dick
s: The Swan Inn fire, a bright red conflagration, interrupts music at the Deanery. It singes Dandy Dick's tail, prompts his rescue and Georgiana's sheltering him there. Hatcham suspects arson, says the Dean set it, and reports a villain caught and taken to the lock-up.

l: the Restoration Fund offer, Dandy Dick
s: The Dean’s thousand-pound Restoration Fund offer attracts seven wealthy matching donors for the Minster Spire, then obliges him to pay his own contribution, causing distress.

l: Noah Topping, Dandy Dick
s: Noah Topping is the rural, ill-fittingly dressed Head Constable of St. Marvells, married to Hannah and running the police station strictly and rigidly. Jealous of Hannah’s male friends, he threatens them and reacts strongly when he finds the Dean with her, locking the Dean in a cell and inventing charges including alienating Hannah’s affections and embezzling his meal. He holds an unknown man in custody, believes this lawful, and plans to take a prisoner to Durnstone after dinner, with a stop to see racing. He first suggests the missing Dean committed suicide, then produces and escorts the handcuffed Dean. Later, dishevelled, he says a lover escaped custody, wrongly identifies the Dean as that man, and is corrected before accepting an invitation to dinner with Hannah.

l: the military summons to St. Marvells, Dandy Dick
s: A military summons to St. Marvells sends the Military away, intended to watch the fire at the Swan; the ball is cancelled; Salome and Sheba enter.

l: gambling on horse races, Dandy Dick
s: takes_place_at St. Marvells [including Tattersall's Ring] Gambling on horse races becomes a possible solution to the Dean's financial problems when Georgiana urges him to stake fifty pounds on Dandy Dick. Blore reveals that he has previously gambled at races and accepts the Dean's money to place the wager.

l: the restoration of the Spire, Dandy Dick
s: The restoration of the Spire urgently needs about a thousand pounds to prevent collapse; lacking funds, Georgiana proposes a Dandy Dick wager to finance immediate work.

l: the Restoration Fund money, Dandy Dick
s: is_intended_for the Restoration Fund [fifty pounds] The Restoration Fund money consists of the fifty pounds the Dean gave Blore to wager on Dandy Dick. Blore instead placed it on Bonny Betsy, which lost.

l: the Bolus, Dandy Dick
s: The Bolus is a simple veterinary remedy for chills, carried in a basin by Hatcham and administered by the Dean to Dandy. Presented as a remedy, it was intended by the Dean to affect the race outcome. Blore secretly introduced a foreign element, and analysis found sixteen grains of strychnine.

l: strychnine, Dandy Dick
s: Strychnine, a poison and chief ingredient of a sixteen-grain bolus, was added by Blore to get Dandy Dick out of the race.

l: Augustin Jedd, Dandy Dick
s: Augustin Jedd is the Dean and Georgiana’s brother. He secretly directs Blore to back Dandy Dick with fifty pounds from the Restoration Fund, then deceives Sir Tristram and his daughters about his absence and the race wager. Detained by police for playing the three-card trick, he is rescued by Georgiana and Sir Tristram after being forcibly taken home from the Hill. He is horrified to discover that a bolus contained strychnine. Noah Topping also alleges that he is Hannah’s unknown lover and holds him in lawful custody before he is rescued, though Hatcham disputes that the man in the stable was the Dean.

l: the police station, Dandy Dick
s: The police station is an auxiliary country station in St. Marvells, partly a kitchen and containing official documents, implements, and a prisoner’s cell. Hannah cooks and admits visitors, Noah works as constable, and Georgiana and Sir Tristram report the Dean’s disappearance. The Dean is held there before transfer to Durnstone.

l: the arrest of the Dean, Dandy Dick
s: The arrest of the Dean follows his being caught administering a dose to Dandy and found trespassing in the Deanery stables. He is taken by cart to the lock-up, held overnight at St. Marvells under the usual rule, then brought from his cell in handcuffs and taken toward Durnstone.

l: the notice cancelling the ball, Dandy Dick
s: The notice cancelling the ball is posted on the front door of the Durnstone Athenaeum and reads, "Ball knocked on the head--Vivat Regina."

l: Hannah Topping, Dandy Dick
s: Hannah Topping, also called Hannah Evans and Mrs. Topping, is a young, skilled cook who formerly served the Dean at the Deanery and is Noah’s wife. At St. Marvells police station, where she cooks, she finds her former master imprisoned. Using the Dean’s whistle and plans involving old Nick, a cart, handcuffs, and a duplicate key, she tries to free and feed him, but Noah discovers the effort and the Dean is returned to his cell. She later admits Georgiana and Sir Tristram, continues arranging escape, and seeks forgiveness and reconciliation with the Dean for Noah.

l: the prisoner's cell, Dandy Dick
s: is_a strong-box [the local name for the cell] The prisoner's cell, called the Strong-box in St. Marvells, is entered through a massive door with a wicket and iron grating. Hannah unlocks it with a duplicate key to release the Dean, and Noah later locks the Dean inside again.

l: the arrested man, Dandy Dick
s: is_accused_of the alleged trespassing and attempted larceny [at the Deanery stables] The arrested man is described in the official book as a person found trespassing in the Deanery stables who refuses to give his name or any account of himself. He is the Dean, though Noah initially does not recognize him.

l: the journey to Durnstone, Dandy Dick
s: uses the cart [driven by Noah Topping] Noah intends to drive the Dean to Durnstone after dinner, using old Nick and passing the edge of the hill to get a glimpse of the racing. Hannah plans for the Dean to escape from the moving cart in Pear Tree Lane, but the plan is not carried out in this unit.

l: crime, Dandy Dick
s: Hannah says that crime levels everyone and believes the Dean's first offence merits giving him another start in life. The Dean insists that he is legally innocent, though he admits to a temporary moral aberration.

l: the alleged trespassing and attempted larceny, Dandy Dick
s: In the third act, the Dean is found trespassing in the Deanery stables, with an alleged intent connected to petty or attempted larceny, though no attempted larceny is proved. Hannah warns of a more serious charge, and Noah additionally accuses the Dean of alienating his wife's affections.

l: old Nick, Dandy Dick
s: Old Nick is a former Durnstone Fire Brigade horse. Noah plans to use him to take a cart quickly toward Durnstone, despite Hannah calling him vicious; his brigade service makes him answer a familiar double whistle. Later Hannah expects him to help bring the Dean back, but Noah leaves him at home.

l: Kitty, Dandy Dick
s: is_in Noah's cart Kitty is put in Noah's cart while Old Nick is left at home. Hannah realizes that this substitution prevents the Dean's planned escape.

l: Noah's cart, Dandy Dick
s: Noah's cart is a vehicle for taking the Dean, Augustin Jedd, to Durnstone, drawn by Old Nick on the journey. It contains Kitty and stands outside the police-station. Hannah's plan has the Dean jump clear and use a whistle while Old Nick runs on, but Noah leaves Old Nick at home.

l: the handcuffs, Dandy Dick
s: are_unlocked_by the duplicate key [after Noah is left behind] Noah selects and examines a pair of handcuffs before preparing to take the prisoner to Durnstone. Hannah gives the Dean a small key that will unlock them once he is free from Noah.

l: the duplicate key, Dandy Dick
s: unlocks the handcuffs [after the arrested man gets free from Noah] Hannah produces a duplicate key to the Strong-box and uses it to unlock the cell door. She later gives the Dean a small key intended to unlock his handcuffs during the planned escape.

l: the Dean's whistle, Dandy Dick
s: The Dean’s whistle, possessed by Augustin Jedd, is Hannah’s whistle. In the third act, Hannah gives it to the Dean and instructs him to blow in Pear Tree Lane and after leaving the cart. Its double-whistle signal summons old Nick to help return him safely to the Deanery.

l: the joint, Dandy Dick
s: is_favored_by Noah Topping [as a meal] The joint is Hannah's cooked meal and Noah's favorite dish. The Dean eats it after escaping from the cell, and Noah treats his eating of it as the embezzling of his midday meal.

l: the Dean's dignity, Dandy Dick
s: is_valued_by the Dean [as a priceless possession of middle age] The Dean calls his dignity a priceless possession of man's middle age. He refuses to notify the Deanery because appearing in the police records and returning publicly would seriously impair it.

l: Hannah's cooking, Dandy Dick
s: is_skillful highly [praised by the Dean] Hannah's cooking is presented as a source of comfort and leverage. The Dean recognizes her culinary skill, eats the joint she prepares, and admits that if every mouthful could carry him back an hour he would finish it.

l: the attempted escape plan, Dandy Dick
s: Hannah proposes that the Dean and Noah ride in a cart, signal at Pear Tree Lane, escape, and free the arrested man with a duplicate key after Noah and old Nick depart. The Dean rejects it, and Noah’s return prevents any attempt.

l: the charge of alienating Hannah's affections, Dandy Dick
s: is_held_against the Dean [by Noah Topping] Noah threatens to add a charge of alienating Hannah's affections to the charges already standing against the Dean. He makes the threat after finding the Dean being served Hannah's cooking.

l: the Dean's disappearance, Dandy Dick
s: is_reported_in the missing-person report Georgiana and Sir Tristram report that Augustin Jedd disappeared after retiring to rest and could not be found in the morning. The disappearance is complicated by the discovery that he is being held in the police-station cell.

l: the Dean's alleged suicide, Dandy Dick
s: is_a theory [Noah's theory] Noah theorizes that the missing Dean's disappearance is an ordinary case of suicide. Georgiana and Sir Tristram reject the idea, and the Dean is subsequently found alive in the cell.

l: the Dean's treatment of Dandy Dick, Dandy Dick
s: is_a simple remedy for chills [administered to a suffering beast] The Dean says he was administering a simple remedy for chills to a suffering beast. Georgiana says the analysis has not yet returned from the chemist, so the treatment's nature is not yet established.

l: the analysis, Dandy Dick
s: identifies strychnine [as sixteen grains in the bolus] The analysis of the bolus is brought to the Deanery by the chemist. It reports that the bolus contains sixteen grains of strychnine, prompting Sir Tristram and Georgiana to denounce the Dean before Blore confesses.

l: the Dean's deception, Dandy Dick
s: The Dean's deception includes hiding his absence and his involvement in the race wager from his family. Salome and Sheba discover that he has stooped to deception, while he also learns that they concealed their attendance at the masked ball and their gambling winnings.

l: the proposed marriages, Dandy Dick
s: Major Tarver proposes to Salome and Mr. Darbey proposes to Sheba; both proposals are accepted. Sir Tristram also proposes to Georgiana, and she agrees to marry him.

l: Deception, Dandy Dick
s: is_a horse [called Deception] Deception is described by the Dean as having frosted the genial summer of the Deanery with the winter of Deceit. Georgiana says that once a person begins to use deception, it takes control and becomes difficult to stop.

l: the horse called Deception, Dandy Dick
s: is_a horse [named Deception] Georgiana compares Deception to a horse that takes the bit between its teeth once it is driven with the whip. She says that the Dean has been riding this horse hardest.

l: laughter at the Dean's expense, Dandy Dick
s: Laughter at the Dean's expense is proposed for a Sporting Dean; Sir Tristram permits it as harmless, while Georgiana limits it to friendly mockery of folly, not virtue, before Noah Topping rushes in dishevelled.

l: Gallegher and Other Stories
s: This document is a collection of short stories centered on New York, Philadelphia, and Monte Carlo characters whose crises are resolved through courage, compassion, reconciliation, or impulsive generosity. It opens with office-boy Gallegher identifying fugitive Stephen S. Hade at Torresdale. He helps Michael E. Dwyer and Detective Hefflefinger seize Hade during an illegal prizefight, then risks arrest and pursuit to bring Dwyer’s report to the Philadelphia Press before deadline; the managing editor restores Gallegher’s position. Young Van Bibber next breaks his engagement, realizes his love for his fiancée, finds her in Central Park, and is understood to become engaged again. Rags Raegen, hiding after striking Pike McGonegal, finds abandoned baby Margaret, struggles to keep her alive, and finally surrenders at the Twenty-first Precinct so she can receive care; months later, he values her affection despite awaiting trial. In “The Other Woman,” the bishop tests Young Latimer’s suitability for Ellen by probing an earlier love. Ellen’s joking intervention turns painful, and Latimer leaves when she rejects his explanation that his past suffering made him worthy. Snipes, a homeless trailer for Alf Wolfe’s gang, helps bring an old farmer and Abraham together, but declines an offer of farm life to remain in New York. The ruined Goodwood Plunger, Cecil Harringford, arrives at Monte Carlo intending suicide, but helping a French couple preserve gambling winnings for a bakery changes him; he decides to return to England. Miss Catherwaight’s investigation of a pawned medal reunites Lewis Lockwood and Judge Burgoyne, former friends divided by a misunderstanding involving her mother. Several Van Bibber stories close the collection: he pays for East Side girls to ride swan-boats, sends an escaped burglar toward his family despite later learning his identity, and ingeniously arranges the eloping Standish and Miss Cambridge’s proper public wedding while misleading Standish’s older brother.

l: Rags Raegen, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Rags Raegen, also called Ragsey or Rags, is a young tough, ice-cart driver, and exceptional underwater swimmer tied to East River and Cherry Street thieves and bullies. Burdened by criminal bonds and a record dating to age ten, he is their hero but eventually shakes the gang's control. After a fight in which he shoots Pike McGonegal, he is pursued by police and accused of murder, though he claims self-defence. He escapes by seeming to drown in the East River and hides in Case's tenement, where he finds the sick, starving baby Margaret. Protecting, feeding, cooling, and comforting her changes him: despite considering flight after learning McGonegal has died, he cannot abandon her. He carries Margaret to the station-house for food and medical attention and voluntarily surrenders. Confined in the Tombs as the case awaits its outcome, he receives daily visits from the baby and later says he does not regret surrendering or leaving the gang, even when he expected to hang.

l: Miss Catherwaight, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Miss Catherwaight is a clever young woman, considered cynical by some friends for her collection of dishonored medals and her remarks about society. Once seen as cold and self-possessed, she travels widely with Mr. Catherwaight and regularly visits pawnshops and loan offices to buy decorations and uncover their histories. Her interest in a silver heart medal leads her to Lewis Lyman Lockwood. Ashamed of intruding into its story, she learns that Lockwood and Burgoyne were separated by a misunderstanding involving her mother. She urges Lockwood to keep the medal and reconcile with Burgoyne, hoping to repair harm her mother caused unwittingly.

l: Van Bibber, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Van Bibber is a twenty-five-year-old New Yorker: a wealthy, popular yet unspoiled young club man, respectable in society, fond of adventure, and possessed of a good heart. Though experienced as a best man or usher, he is not practised at lying. His emotional story begins when he breaks off his engagement and tells himself he should remain a bachelor. Remembering the three months with his fiancée, he realizes she was the source of his happiness, returns with the ring to their secluded place in Central Park, and rushes to her when he finds her there. On a hot day in the Park, initially cross and sleepy, he pays for three East Side girls to ride the swan-boats, accompanies them, shows them the sights, and buys them more tickets. After confronting and disarming a burglar, he chooses not to surrender him; instead he sends him west to Helena with a ticket and money, later learning the man was the escaped Abe Hubbard, alias Jimmie the Gent. Finally, as Cortlandt Van Bibber, he protects young Standish's elopement with Miss Cambridge through a false claim, organizes their formal wedding, and serves as best man, though he regrets where he sent Standish's brother.

l: Gallegher, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Gallegher is a young office-boy at the Press, living alone with his mother in a little house in the extreme northern part of Philadelphia. Short, broad, solid, muscular, and perpetually smiling, he has bright black eyes, street-trained knowledge, and an unusually developed talent for detection. His chief interest is crime: he knows criminals’ aliases, methods, imprisonment, whereabouts, and transgressions, and knows the officers of the twenty-second police district by name. He recognizes Stephen S. Hade from a possibly artificial finger, follows him from Kensington railroad station to Torresdale and the Eagle Inn, telegraphs Detective Hefflefinger, and brings the discovery to Michael E. Dwyer. He joins Dwyer and Hefflefinger, directs their cab, plans an escape route, enters Keppler’s barn, watches from a haymow, and helps identify and secure Hade. When Dwyer’s notebook must reach the Press, Gallegher takes it, deceives the gate officers, flees by cab, and drives through the night toward Philadelphia. Delayed, wet, exhausted, and nearly unable to stand, he reaches the Press with Dwyer’s copy, reports Hade’s capture and Dwyer’s arrest, and proudly says he beat the town.

l: the Press, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The Press is a newspaper in Philadelphia. It employs Gallegher as an office-boy, but its managing editor discharges him for repeated truancy; Dwyer plans to seek his reinstatement after Gallegher discovers Hade. Late at night, its editors and compositors prepare the paper and await news of a fight and Hade’s arrest. The sporting editor sends a message, Dwyer acts as the Press’s representative, and payment depends on no other paper learning of the arrest. Gallegher races to deliver Dwyer’s notebook but is stopped seven blocks from the office.

l: Philadelphia, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Philadelphia is the city where Gallegher lives and works, with detailed knowledge of its police districts, criminals, and transportation. It lies about four miles south of the raid, glows faint yellow in the sky, is near Torresdale and the Eagle Inn, and is reached by Gallegher while delivering a report.

l: Richard F. Burrbank, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Richard F. Burrbank is a prominent, very wealthy New York railroad lawyer and railroad-stock owner, considered for many high offices, whose record ends with his being found dead from two pistol wounds above his heart.

l: the Burrbank murder, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The Burrbank murder is an internationally reported investigation into Richard F. Burrbank’s killing, safe opening and $200,000 theft, with his secretary Stephen S. Hade suspected and missing.

l: Hade, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Hade, Richard F. Burrbank’s secretary, is suspected of Burrbank’s murder and the safe burglary on circumstantial evidence. After Burrbank’s death, he disappears, hiding near Torresdale as Mr. Carleton and using the alias Arlie Lane. Missing the right trigger finger shot off in childhood, he attends a fight in disguise, fearing Keppler and the risk of staying away. During a police raid, Hefflefinger seizes him; Hade offers money and part of his fortune for release, but is identified as the murderer, arrested, and captured.

l: the Champion of the United States, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: opposes the Would-be Champion [in the big fight] The Champion of the United States is scheduled to take part in a major fight near Philadelphia.

l: the Would-be Champion, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The Would-be Champion is scheduled to fight the Champion of the United States near Philadelphia.

l: the Heenan-Sayers fight, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The Heenan-Sayers fight is a heavily publicized contest between the Champion of the United States and the Would-be Champion, scheduled near Philadelphia in the Eagle Inn barn with $250 tickets. Editors await confirmation, initially doubting it occurred, until Gallegher brings the report. Correspondents urgently describe the fight and Hade’s final capture; afterward, the correspondents are arrested, and Captain Scott cites the fight as evidence that they broke the peace.

l: Detective Hefflefinger, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Detective Hefflefinger is a detective on Inspector Byrnes’s staff and in Byrnes’s detective force, carrying a badge and warrant. He comes to Philadelphia seeking a burglar, but the burglar has escaped. After Gallegher reports that Hade is near Torresdale, Hefflefinger agrees to arrest Hade quietly under a burglary pretext. He enters a barn, watches Hade during a fight, captures and handcuffs him in a police raid, rejects his bribe, and plans to take him to the station and then New York.

l: Inspector Byrnes, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Inspector Byrnes supervises the detective staff to which Detective Hefflefinger belongs.

l: New York, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: New York is a crowded, harsh place linked by trains and marked by the Bowery, Broadway, Thirty-fifth Street, pawnshops, loan offices, drug-store and cigar-store post-offices, vice, crime, poverty, and green-goods operations. Its scattered private post-offices are said to make vice and crime easy. It is repeatedly a destination and setting for danger: Richard F. Burrbank is murdered there, Hade is to be taken there after a planned arrest, and secrecy depends on newspapers there learning nothing. Snipes knows the city but refuses to exchange it for the country. After Mrs. Catherwaight's death, Miss Catherwaight's father and daughter live and entertain there while she searches for medals. At dawn, Van Bibber returns from Jersey City through nearly deserted streets; a reporter calls the city exciting yet brutal and commonplace, shaped by recurring crime and poverty. Van Bibber then helps a burglar leave by train.

l: Kensington railroad station, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_in Philadelphia [near Gallegher's home] Kensington railroad station is near Gallegher's home and has trains running toward the suburbs and New York. Gallegher sees the suspected Hade there, follows him, and boards the train to Torresdale.

l: Torresdale, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Torresdale is a station outside Philadelphia on the Pennsylvania Railroad, near the old Eagle Inn. It matters as the site where suspected Hade gets off, Gallegher arranges Detective Hefflefinger’s meeting, and plans are made to take Hade away on the one o’clock train. A cab reaches Torresdale; nearby, at Keppler’s barn, Hade is arrested after a fight.

l: the old Eagle Inn, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_a old roadside hostelry [known as a headquarters for pothunters and a battle-ground of cock-fights] The Eagle Inn is an old roadside hostelry near Torresdale known as a gathering place for pothunters and cock-fights. The suspected Hade, using the name Mr. Carleton, is staying there, and the big fight is scheduled in its barn.

l: Mr. Carleton, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Mr. Carleton is the assumed name of a well-dressed, gloved man staying at the Eagle Inn for his health; he acts nervously when asked about a fight, and Gallegher believes he is Stephen S. Hade.

l: Michael E. Dwyer, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Michael E. Dwyer is the sporting editor of the Press. After hearing Gallegher’s important report, he plans and joins a quiet trip to Torresdale with Gallegher and Detective Hefflefinger to secure Hade’s secret arrest, protect the story from competing papers, offer and share a $500 reward, and recommend Gallegher’s reinstatement.

l: the police, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The police raid Keppler’s barn during a fight, break down doors, and trigger panic. They hem in and arrest newspaper correspondents and others, guard the gate, use patrol-wagons for prisoners, and permit Hefflefinger through after he shows a badge. After Gallegher escapes, an officer fires shots; city officers later stop his cab for unlit lamps and let it continue.

l: the $5,000 reward, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The $5,000 reward is offered for Hade’s capture and delivery to the police. Dwyer says it will belong to Gallegher if Hade is caught, then offers Hefflefinger part of it for a secret arrest that keeps other newspapers uninformed.

l: the stolen fortune, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The stolen fortune is $200,000 in bonds, stocks, and money, placed in Burrbank's safe the night before the murder and then taken.

l: Hade's arrest, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Hade's arrest is a secretly planned capture intended to avoid publicity from other newspapers. Gallegher and Michael E. Dwyer arrange for Detective Hefflefinger to seize the suspected Hade near the Eagle Inn after the fight and take him to New York on the one o'clock train. During a police raid, Hefflefinger uses his badge and a false burglary explanation to remove Hade from the barn. Editors waiting for confirmation are told by Gallegher that Hade was captured.

l: the Burrbank murder investigation, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The investigation has produced a worldwide search for Stephen S. Hade, whose description was circulated by telegraph and cable. People suspected of being Hade have been arrested in various places, but Gallegher's discovery near Torresdale offers a possible breakthrough.

l: Mr. Dwyer, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Mr. Dwyer is a Press representative and newspaper correspondent serving as sporting editor. During a raid, he writes in Dwyer’s notebook, identifies himself to Hefflefinger, and offers $500 for Hade’s secret arrest as the supposed burglar. He enters Keppler’s barn, remains near Hade during the fight, and signals or identifies him. After Captain Scott orders the correspondents arrested, Dwyer resists, entrusts Gallegher with his notebook and report, and is arrested; Gallegher delivers Dwyer’s prepared copy to the Press.

l: the sporting crowd, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_composed_of sporting men [including club-men, brokers, politicians, comedians, amateur boxers, and others] The sporting crowd consists of sporting men, club-men, brokers, politicians, a comedian and his manager, amateur boxers, and others from cities around the country. Its members bet heavily, crowd around the ring, react violently to the fight, and panic when the police raid begins.

l: the fighters, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: are two prizefighters [physical combatants in the fight] The fighters enter the ring after the crowd has gathered and begin a brutal, closely contested bout. One fighter loses favor as the fight continues, while the other gains the advantage through repeated severe blows.

l: the barn (Keppler's barn), Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Keppler’s barn is a large building containing stalls, haymows, a ring, and a crowd gathered for an illegal fight. Gallegher and Hefflefinger enter through a window, and the police later raid it during the bout.

l: McGovern's cab, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: McGovern's cab, kept at Bachman's livery stable and associated with Luke McGovern, carries the sporting editor and Gallegher through a cold, snowy journey to Torresdale. It waits near the lower gate with its lamps out for a rapid departure. Later Gallegher finds it at the furthermost gate, frees it, and drives toward Philadelphia, where cabmen stop it and question him.

l: Gallegher's horse, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: pulls McGovern's cab [while driven by Gallegher] Gallegher's horse is chilled after standing in the cold but eagerly pulls the cab through the night. It carries him recklessly toward Philadelphia until the cabmen seize its head near the Press office.

l: the train, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: departs_for New York [at 1.20] The train passing the Torresdale station at 1.20 is intended to carry Hade secretly toward New York after his arrest. Hefflefinger plans to take that train with him.

l: the burglary, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The burglary is the supposed offense used to conceal Hade’s true arrest. Hefflefinger tells the police that Hade is the burglar “Arlie” Lane, alias Carleton, and says he has papers authorizing the arrest.

l: the fight, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_a prizefighting [a secret bare-fist contest] The fight is held in Keppler’s barn before a carefully selected sporting crowd. It is a prolonged and exceptionally brutal contest, interrupted when the police break into the barn.

l: the police raid, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The police raid targets a fight at the barn. It begins when barn doors are forced open, causing panic that scatters spectators; Hefflefinger seizes Hade and leaves. As the raid settles down, officers hold and arrest newspaper correspondents, amid disorder that lets Gallegher attempt to carry away the report.

l: the $500 payment, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The $500 payment is the amount Dwyer promises Hefflefinger from the $5,000 reward for secretly arresting Hade. Hefflefinger expects to receive it after carrying out the plan.

l: the boxing ring, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_a square fighting enclosure [covered with sawdust and bounded by a heavy rope] The boxing ring is a square enclosure formed by wooden posts and heavy rope, with sawdust covering its floor. The two fighters battle inside it while the crowd presses around the ropes.

l: prizefighting, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Prizefighting draws the crowd to Keppler’s barn despite the storm and the threat of police interference. The illegal bout provides the setting in which Hade is located and arrested.

l: Captain Scott, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Captain Scott, a captain in charge of a raid, has newspaper correspondents arrested, declares they are under arrest, orders them taken to the station-house, and refuses release because they were under bonds to keep the peace and had fought again.

l: newspaper correspondents, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Newspaper correspondents, representing principal papers, are under peace bonds yet involved in a fight during a raid; as it settles, they demand to send reports, and Captain Scott arrests them for a station-house hearing.

l: police patrol-wagons, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: transport arrests of the newspaper men [to the station-house] Three police patrol-wagons move through the yard carrying unwilling prisoners packed together without protection from the sleet and rain. One patrol-wagon pursues Gallegher after he escapes, but he believes it is likely to become stuck in the mud.

l: arrests of the newspaper men, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Captain Scott orders the newspaper men taken into custody and sent to the station-house for a magistrate's hearing. The arrests threaten to delay their reports beyond the deadline for the next day's paper.

l: the Press office, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The Press office is Gallegher's destination for delivering Dwyer's report. It is only seven blocks away when the cabmen stop him, and Gallegher insists that its staff will prove his story and pay for the cab's trip.

l: Dwyer's notebook, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Dwyer’s notebook contains his written account of the fight, including Gallegher’s work and Hade’s final capture. While the raid settles, Dwyer writes in it; Gallegher takes it from Dwyer’s coat, carries it toward the Press office, then hands over its damp, limp-covered copy.

l: the newspaper report of the fight, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The newspaper report of the fight is the material Gallegher is trying to deliver before the printing forms are locked. Its timely arrival would allow the paper to beat the town and the country.

l: the patrol-wagon pursuit, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: pursues Gallegher's ride to the Press office [after Gallegher escapes the raid site] The patrol-wagon pursuit begins after Gallegher escapes from the raided house in McGovern's cab. Its gong and red and green lanterns follow him through the darkness, but the wagon falls behind as he drives toward Philadelphia.

l: managing editor, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The managing editor of the Press uses a speaking-tube to tell the night editor there is no news, then orders printing to begin. When Gallegher arrives, he handles Dwyer’s copy, tends to the wet boy, and says he will not be dismissed.

l: night editor, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The Press’s night editor, in the composing-room, repeatedly presses for news, urges printing rather than delay, and ends disappointed when Gallegher arrives.

l: city editor, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: A city editor in local and reportorial rooms seeks news, then helps a cab-driver support Gallegher into the composing-room and orders brandy.

l: Mr. Dwyer's copy, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_in notebook Gallegher delivers Mr. Dwyer's copy to the managing editor. The managing editor passes it to the foreman, who tears out its leaves and distributes them to the compositors.

l: news, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The managing editor repeatedly answers that there is no news, and the city editor asks for an update. News finally arrives with Gallegher, who brings word of Mr. Dwyer's arrest and Hade's capture.

l: story, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The editors hesitate to delay the paper for a purely hypothetical story. The night editor argues that if there were a story to print, Mr. Dwyer would have delivered it sooner.

l: printing the paper, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_delayed past the scheduled time [by the uncertainty about the story] The Press begins printing after the managing editor agrees that the paper cannot wait any longer. The foreman starts giving orders, but the arrival of Mr. Dwyer's copy allows the compositors to set the new material.

l: Van Bibber's fiancée, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Van Bibber's fiancée is a young, lovely, cultured woman, knowledgeable about the Louvre, painters, and cathedrals. After accepting a breakup and returning her engagement ring, she goes to their secluded box-bush dell, tearful, kisses a sprig of box, and is approached by Van Bibber.

l: the engagement and breakup, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: An engagement lasting three months of continual companionship ends when Van Bibber tries to make it appear his fiancée chose the separation. Regretting the breakup, he seeks her in a secluded dell; they reconcile and are seen driving home together.

l: the Avenue, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_a city avenue [through which Young Van Bibber walks northward] The Avenue is where Van Bibber walks north after leaving his fiancée. As he passes its streets, carriages and familiar club acquaintances prompt him to reflect on his former social life and on what he has lost.

l: Central Park, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Central Park is a place with a secluded box-bush dell, a lake, paths, bushes, an artificial lake, and nearby stables. Van Bibber enters it grieving a breakup and crosses the turf toward the secluded place where he and his fiancée met. Later, in hot weather, he waits for his groom and moves to a shaded bench near the lake.

l: the secluded box-bush dell, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: A secluded, pretty Central Park spot, marked by a circle of box and a green bench beneath a box bush, is Van Bibber and his fiancée’s favorite meeting place. He arrives intending to bury the engagement ring, but finds her beneath the bush breaking off a sprig.

l: Abraham's trip to New York, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Abraham travels to New York on the first train with the $200 he saved. After the Deacon permits him to marry Kate without requiring $2,000, he goes to buy a ring, not counterfeit money.

l: marriage, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Marriage is briefly rejected by Young Van Bibber after his fiancée pales on him after three months; he concludes he is not meant for it and imagines bachelorhood, but a reunion with her suggests that conclusion may not hold.

l: the engagement, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The engagement has lasted three months of close companionship before Van Bibber ends it. After he finds his fiancée in their old meeting place, they are observed returning together in her brougham and are described as engaged.

l: Margaret, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Margaret is a female baby left in a tenement room while her parents are imprisoned on Blackwell's Island. She lies in bedding, needs milk, and is weakened by heat, inadequate food, and lack of care; deep blue rings surround her closed eyes, and her breathing becomes dangerously irregular. At first she uncertainly recognizes Rags Raegen, then greets him with smiles, coos, affection, and trust. Raegen gives her water and softened bread, watches over her through the night, and carries her to the station-house when she becomes ill after two days without food. A char-woman gives her milk and arranges medical care. After the Society rejects her family as caretakers, Raegen cares for her. Later, she visits him in the Tombs, reaches for him, and kisses him through the bars.

l: Pike McGonegal, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Pike McGonegal, a darling and hero of the Thirty-third Street tenements, is reported murdered by Ragsey Raegen. Raegen says McGonegal drew a pistol and was struck in self-defense; a cop supports the pistol claim.

l: police, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Police pursue Rags Raegen after he strikes McGonegal and falls. They block the East River, search Case's tenement and its roofs with a revolver, question one another, and fail to find him beneath bedding. As Rags considers escape, police watch ferries, railway depots, and a river boat to intercept departing criminals.

l: Case's tenement, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Case's tenement is a dark, mostly empty, largely untenanted building with few chances to move between rooms. While fleeing, Rags enters and eventually hides in a nearly bare room, where he encounters Margaret. It contains room No. 8, rented by green-goods men who receive visiting countrymen.

l: the rooftops, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: are_unfamiliar_to Rags Raegen [in Thirty-third Street] The rooftops are unfamiliar territory for Rags, unlike the roofs in his own neighborhood. Police pursue him across them, and Italians watching from nearby windows point him out to an officer, forcing him to retreat into the building.

l: the tenement building's interior, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The building's dark, narrow interior has stairways, a roof ladder, and a small room with bedding, scant food, and whiskey. It offers little shelter: Rags runs upstairs, falls over a bucket, retreats from the roof, and hides from police in a room.

l: Rags's escape and hiding, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Rags’s escape and hiding unfolds during a police pursuit in Case’s tenement. He drops from a rooftop through a wooden trap, hides beneath bedding in a dark room, and remains still while police inspect it. Though he considers boatmen to Astoria or the Jersey shore, changing his name, and working elsewhere, Margaret’s condition keeps him concealed overnight as he cares for her.

l: Rags's pursuit by police, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: leads_to the rooftops [after the river escape route is blocked] Rags is pursued because the police saw him strike McGonegal and saw McGonegal fall. They close in on him from the stairs and roof, while another officer watches from the street, but Rags avoids capture.

l: Rags's fight with McGonegal, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Rags's fight with McGonegal was a street assault witnessed by police: Rags struck McGonegal, causing him to fall. It led to police pursuit and a criminal charge. Rags says he acted in self-defense, citing witnesses who saw McGonegal pull a pistol, and expects a short sentence.

l: the police pursuit of Raegen, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The police pursuit of Raegen lasts two days. Police chase Rags through a building and over roofs, search rooms with revolvers, and leave believing him hidden under bedding. Detectives later find Raegen at the station-house, where he gives himself up after giving them a chase.

l: bedding, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: conceals Rags Raegen [during the police search] Rags dives beneath a pile of tossed-up bedding and presses himself against the wall to avoid detection. After the police leave, he gathers the bedding over himself again while listening, and later uses it as a place to sit while holding Margaret.

l: the ward detectives, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Ward detectives pursue Ragsey Raegen on suspicion, investigate with McGonegal's friends Wade and Heffner, and watch a tenement from across the street, causing Rags to remain inside while they are nearby.

l: the Twenty-first Precinct station-house, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: contains the reading-room The Twenty-first Precinct station-house receives Raegen when he brings in the sick and starving baby. Its sergeant, reserve squad, char-woman, and detectives become involved in caring for the baby and identifying Raegen.

l: the sun, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The sun rises hissing from the East River as a broad, red disc of heat, sweeping the city with a man-of-war search-light glare; its light enters open windows and dangerously heats baby's bedding.

l: heat, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: causes Ragsey Raegen [with sleeplessness and whiskey contributing] The heat makes Rags ache and causes his eyes to smart, while Margaret gasps, weakens, and develops dark rings around her eyes. Rags cools her with water and fans her, but the heat contributes to his exhaustion and stupor.

l: milk, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_used_for Margaret [as desired nourishment] Rags believes milk is the food babies need and plans to obtain some from a passing milk-cart. Because he cannot get outside safely, he gives Margaret moistened ham and bread instead.

l: murder of Pike McGonegal, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_reported_by evening newspapers [as a full account] A newsboy announces a full account of the murder of Pike McGonegal by Ragsey Raegen. The announcement terrifies Rags, though he maintains that the killing was self-defense.

l: McGonegal's shooting, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_claimed_as self-defence [by Ragsey Raegen] Rags says he struck McGonegal after McGonegal pulled a gun on him. He maintains that he acted in self-defense, while the newspaper describes McGonegal's death as murder.

l: Rags's criminal record, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_kept_in Police Court [on Police Court blotters] Rags knows that his life history has been recorded in Police Court blotters since he was ten years old. He believes his record, his enemies, and his limited friends make secret and immediate flight his safest option.

l: the surly old sergeant, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The surly old sergeant of the Twenty-first Precinct station-house, believing he has humor, answers Raegen facetiously, rejects using the station-house as dispensary or foundling hospital, then summons reserves and the char-woman after threats.

l: the char-woman, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The char-woman, caretaker at the Twenty-first Precinct station-house, responds when an ill baby is brought downstairs. Taking the baby in her arms, she says heat and poor care caused its condition, orders milk, a surgeon, and ice, and insists it will not die.

l: the gang, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Raegen later says that he has shaken the gang.

l: the Society, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: has_decided the baby's family is unfit to care for the baby Raegen says that the Society has decided that the baby's family is not fit to take care of her.

l: the Tombs, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Raegen says that he sat in the Tombs expecting to hang while the case against him was going badly. The baby was brought to visit him there every day.

l: Raegen's surrender, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_a voluntary surrender [to the police] Raegen's surrender occurs when he brings the baby to the station-house and gives himself up. He insists that nobody captured him.

l: the case against Raegen, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_serious capital case [Raegen expects to hang] Raegen says that the case was once going dead against him and that he expected to hang in the Tombs. He refers to a cop swearing to McGonegal's drawing the pistol.

l: the baby's illness and starvation, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_caused_by inadequate care The baby becomes ill from the heat and has not eaten for two days, leaving her half-starved. The char-woman gives her milk, orders ice to be prepared, and summons the surgeon; she says the baby will not die.

l: Latimer, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Latimer is a young man, known well to the bishop and a frequent visitor to his study, who loves Ellen deeply and seeks to marry her. He presents himself as professionally established, self-respecting, and personally disinclined to dissipation, denying wild oats, anonymous letters, or any damaging past account. Yet he has loved another woman in a former forbidden relationship and remains separated from her. When the bishop raises a thirty-day hypothetical, Latimer refuses to answer, protests that its conditions are impossible, and says the other woman is neither dead nor available to a man like him, perhaps being married. He insists that he now prefers and loves Ellen above all else, believing God sent her as a reward. In pleading with Ellen, he says he overcame the earlier love by refusing to yield to it, and that the struggle made him honest, clean, and worthy of her. When Ellen tells him to go to the other woman, he leaves, turning away from the north where she is located toward rooms in the south.

l: Ellen, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Ellen is the bishop’s only daughter, a woman loved by young Latimer, whom she loves and intends to marry if her father agrees. Her father sees her future happiness as his responsibility and fears she would suffer if Latimer loved another woman again. Ellen initially teases Latimer for seeming afraid before he speaks to the bishop. After secretly testing him as a joke meant to frighten him, she enters distressed and exhausted, asks her father to send Latimer away, and tells Latimer to go to the other woman.

l: Ellen's father, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Ellen’s father is a bishop and priest, young for his high office, and Ellen’s sole surviving parent, guardian, and caregiver. Concerned about her future after she leaves his household, he knows Latimer’s family and likes young Latimer. When Latimer proposes marriage, he listens closely but tests whether Latimer’s past, especially another woman, could endanger Ellen’s happiness; Latimer’s refusal to answer a hypothetical convinces him that it reveals a true feeling. Later, after hearing Latimer explain his past and feelings, he pities Ellen, judges Latimer honorable, says he would have been proud to hear such words from a son, urges Ellen to understand him, and watches Latimer depart with sympathy and concern.

l: the bishop's study, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The bishop's study is a richly furnished room with hundreds of books, pictures, etchings, plaster casts, dark red curtains, an open fire, ferns, and blue-and-white plaques. There, the bishop and young Latimer hold an extended conversation about Ellen's future.

l: the marriage proposal, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Young Latimer proposes marriage to Ellen through her father, telling the bishop that Ellen has agreed if her father does not oppose. He says he loves her and believes he can make her happy.

l: Latimer and Ellen's love, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_mutual love Young Latimer says that Ellen has become essential to his happiness and that a day without seeing her is wasted and discontented. He says that he loves her so deeply that making her happy is his chief desire. Ellen has told him that she loves him.

l: Latimer's past, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Latimer's past is examined for hidden dangers to Ellen. Young Latimer says he lived as other young men did but avoided dissipation as vulgar, and denies wild oats, an ugly story, an unreturned consequence, or any woman who could expose him by letter or accusation.

l: Latimer's future with Ellen, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Latimer envisions a long, quiet future with Ellen, including marriage and honorable ambition. He imagines using his position and resources to provide her comfort, pleasure, and charitable opportunities. The bishop agrees her material security would be assured, but worries that Latimer may not shield her from past consequences.

l: the test by hypothetical conditions, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: A test based on hypothetical conditions asks young Latimer to imagine thirty days before death with no moral or legal consequences, then choose between Ellen and another woman. The bishop treats Latimer’s refusal as an answer. Ellen used the trick to learn what he would say about his past love. Latimer condemns it as impossible, unjust, needless, and horrible, saying it confuses them by treating the unreal and impossible as significant.

l: the other woman, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The other woman is alive and possibly married. Latimer loved her in the past, but they renounced their love when it became a crime or impossible, and she may have suffered silently. He suggests he might love her again if the obstacle between them ended.

l: love between Latimer and the other woman, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: This is Latimer’s past love for another woman, suppressed and sacrificed by both. Though he says overcoming it made him honest and worthy and insists he loves Ellen certainly above all else, the bishop raises that changed circumstances could revive the love after Latimer marries Ellen. Latimer calls the woman beyond the love of a man like himself, making it a forbidden or impossible temptation.

l: marriage, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_possible_between Latimer [with Ellen as his wife] The bishop warns that marriage to Ellen could occur before the obstacle separating Latimer from the other woman ended, making any later trouble difficult to remedy. Latimer suggests that the other woman may already be a married woman.

l: Snipes, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Snipes is a very young, homeless, imperfectly trained but skilled trailer for the green-goods men, paid a quarter per shadowed victim. Unnoticeable in crowds, patient, and able to follow men through changing streets, he resists compulsory reform. He aids and sympathizes with an old farmer, protects Abraham, reaches Grand Central Depot, and declines farm life to remain in New York.

l: Alf Wolfe, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Alf Wolfe, using the name Perceval, leads green-goods men from rented room No. 8; when confronted by an old farmer, he overpowers but releases him.

l: the old farmer, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: A strict-living father from a simple country family, he hosts city children at his farm, seeks Abraham in New York over counterfeit money, confronts Wolfe, reunites with Abraham, and invites Snipes home.

l: Abraham, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Abraham, the old farmer’s son, saves $200 for marriage, becomes engaged to Kate with the old Deacon’s consent, and goes to New York to buy a ring despite his father’s counterfeit-money suspicion.

l: the green-goods men, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Green-goods men rent room No. 8, circulate counterfeit-money offers, then arrange meetings to watch and rob suspected customers; Alf Wolfe leads, with Snipes trailing.

l: room No. 8, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Room No. 8 is the rented headquarters where Alf Wolfe and the green-goods men meet prospective customers. The old farmer enters it looking for Abraham and confronts Wolfe, but Abraham is not there.

l: the Bowery, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: contains pawnshops and loan offices The Bowery is where Miss Catherwaight finds the silver heart medal in a pawnbroker's window among razors, pistols, and family Bibles. She is well known to the pawnshops and loan offices there, whose proprietors save medals for her and try to learn or invent their histories.

l: Grand Central station, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Grand Central station, also called Grand Central Depot, is a railway station where tickets are sold. Van Bibber brings a burglar there and buys him a ticket for Helena, Montana. It is also where Snipes takes an exhausted old farmer, who unexpectedly reunites with Abraham before they prepare to return home.

l: green goods, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_a technical name for counterfeit bills Green goods is the technical term for counterfeit bills. The green-goods men offer countrymen large amounts of it in exchange for smaller amounts of legitimate money, claiming that the only victim is the Government.

l: counterfeit money, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_offered_for $500 [$5,000 worth offered] Counterfeit money is what the green-goods men claim to sell to their customers. The old farmer mistakenly believes Abraham has come to New York to spend $200 on $2,000 worth of counterfeit money.

l: the trailer's work, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The trailer's work is to shadow a prospective customer from the first meeting with the green-goods men to a later meeting and report any suspicious behavior. Snipes is skilled at remaining unnoticed, following people through crowds, and alerting Wolfe if a customer appears to be a detective.

l: Young Harringford (Cecil, the Goodwood Plunger), Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Young Harringford, Cecil, is a young man known publicly as the Goodwood Plunger or The Plunger. Eldest son of the Harringford family, he is estranged from and effectively disinherited by his father after gambling losses, debts, and disgrace, though they still love one another. Loved by the girl from Surrey and attended by the longtime servant Walters, Cecil reaches Monte Carlo in worsening mental and physical distress. Having lost his fortune and unable to cover his debts, he seeks a final second chance through the Grand Prix and the English horse; if it fails, he plans suicide in Monte Carlo, away from home. There he is regarded as fortunate and rich by a distressed woman, who asks him to stop her husband Louis from gambling. Cecil learns Louis has won money but is risking it, intervenes, divides the winnings for separate bets, takes the money from the table, and places it in the woman's skirt. He sends the couple to Paris, abandons his suicidal course, and plans to return to England by the first available train with Walters.

l: Harringford's father, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Harringford's father rejects Young Harringford after gambling disgraces the family name, but later recognizes his error. Through Walters, he invites Cecil home, offering reconciliation and declaring him dearer than his other sons. He depends on Cecil to continue the family line and hopes his return will make him happy.

l: the girl from Surrey, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: A girl from Surrey living near the Harringford family estate is an important object of Young Harringford’s affection. During her illness, he watches her lighted window and longs to meet her again. She openly asks after him despite social judgment, showing concern as he comes to Monte Carlo in a changed state of mind.

l: Walters, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Walters, Cecil Harringford's longstanding, deeply devoted servant, is found handling a letter to Cecil's father, helps pack for Cecil's departure, feels relieved by the decision to leave, and watches over Cecil as he falls asleep longing for home.

l: Monte Carlo, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Monte Carlo is a place containing a Casino and gambling at its tables. Harringford comes from Paris intending to die there, choosing it because it differs from home and because he recalls a young Russian who killed himself after losing at the tables; he waits outside the Casino late at night. During a marriage tour, a woman and Louis are there, though she says gambling tables are not for people like them and they must return to Paris next day. A Frenchman gambles there until Cecil urges him and his wife to leave that night, having seen arrivals rich depart paupers.

l: Casino at Monte Carlo, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Casino at Monte Carlo is a place with green gambling tables and lights. Young Harringford, the “Goodwood Plunger,” stands by a pillar, watching the lights and waiting for closing. In a changed state of mind, he intends to die there after the lights are extinguished, considering the Casino a fitting setting.

l: Surrey, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Surrey is the home of Harringford’s family and the setting of the neighboring estate where the girl lives. Harringford remembers its fields, trout springs, park, and terraces, and longs to return there despite believing that he has lost the right to do so.

l: Paris, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Paris is the couple's destination after Cecil sends them away from Monte Carlo. They are expected to arrive there by morning and return to their home and shop.

l: Grand Prix, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_the_setting_for Siren's race [the final gambling coup] The Grand Prix is Harringford’s final gambling coup, on which he stakes his hopes of restoring his fortune, reconciling with his father, and seeing the girl again. The English horse fails to win, as Frou Frou passes the goal, and Harringford returns to Paris in despair.

l: gambling and debt, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: causes Harringford's mental and physical distress [through financial loss, disgrace, and isolation] Harringford begins gambling after coming into his money and secretly backs Siren with enormous sums, winning a fortune at the Goodwood Cup. His later losses bring visits to lenders, borrowing, threats of executions, and debts he cannot repay, culminating in the failed Grand Prix wager.

l: Harringford's mental and physical distress, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: includes fear of mental collapse [recurring and increasingly terrifying] Harringford suffers a numb feeling and sharp pain in his head, trembling nerves, twitching, loss of appetite, shivering, insomnia, and fear that his mind is failing. He repeatedly tests whether his speech and thoughts are sensible and believes that only death can stop the pain, doubts, and terror.

l: Harringford's planned suicide, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_intended_to_end Harringford's mental and physical distress [as an escape from pain, fear, and inability to rest] Harringford decides that he will kill himself at Monte Carlo if his final gambling coup fails. He believes suicide will bring rest and peace, feels that others would understand if they experienced his suffering, and waits for the Casino lights to go out before acting.

l: Harringford's father's letter, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Harringford’s father writes to Young Harringford, offering peace, forgiveness, and a welcome home. Invoking the Prodigal Son, he says Cecil, his first-born, is dearer than the other ninety-nine and that the girl from Surrey still asks about him. In Monte Carlo, Harringford reads the letter for the last time and tears it up.

l: woman (the Goodwood Plunger's interlocutor), Gallegher and Other Stories
s: A pretty, rather short, plainly dressed French bourgeois woman is newly married to Louis and has no friends in Monte Carlo. Though she has dowry money for part of Carbut's bakery store, Louis's roulette winnings are crucial to paying their debt and creating the independent little shop she wants. She begs the Goodwood Plunger, Cecil, to stop Louis from gambling further. After receiving the winnings, she and Louis go to Paris, own a shop, and she gratefully credits Cecil with helping secure their happier future.

l: Louis, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Louis is a handsome young Frenchman, husband, apprentice to old Carbut in baking, and owner of a third of Carbut's bakery store. Though not usually a gambler, he plays dominoes at cafes and, at Monte Carlo, wins money at roulette, including 20,000 francs. Excited by repeated bets on red, he risks his winnings hoping to buy another third of the store. Cecil stops his final all-in gamble; Louis leaves for Paris with his wife, grateful, humble, and resolved never to return to Monte Carlo.

l: Carbut's bakery store, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Carbut's bakery store is a bakery partly owned by apprentice Louis, who holds a third. Old Carbut offers the remainder for 20,000 francs so he can retire, but Louis's gambling jeopardizes the couple's purchase.

l: gambling, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: takes_place_at Monte Carlo [at the tables] Gambling at the tables has caused Louis to become excited and reckless despite his usual lack of interest in gambling. He has won a large amount but continues risking it instead of stopping, and the woman asks the Goodwood Plunger to persuade him to quit.

l: money, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Money, saved by a woman with Louis through months or years of hard work, includes a dowry that paid for part of Carbut's bakery store. Louis wins money needed to buy the rest, but risks losing it by continuing to gamble.

l: casino gambling, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: includes roulette game Casino gambling is shown as dangerous because the Frenchman nearly risks all of the couple's money even after winning a large sum. Cecil intervenes because he has seen gamblers become paupers.

l: roulette game, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The roulette game limits each person to 6,000 francs and uses red as an outcome. It unfolds with successive Frenchman wins on red, ending when seven brings Cecil a larger combined win before another wager is stopped.
